extracted.intended_audience: General readers, students, and researchers interested in architecture, urban planning, public housing, and St. Louis history
extracted.subtask_description: A Wikipedia encyclopedic overview of the Wendell O. Pruitt Homes and William Igoe Apartments (Pruitt–Igoe) covering design, construction, history, decline, demolition, causes of failure, and legacy. The page aggregates historical facts, contemporary commentary, and scholarly interpretations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Architectural form and layout (high-rise design)
rubrics_metrics.description: The complex consisted of 33 eleven-story concrete apartment buildings in the modernist/International Style; design choices included uniform 11-floor height imposed by federal cost limits and the 'towers in the park' concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether high-rise towers are appropriate for low-income family housing: the article cites that the huge 11‑story buildings were 'reportedly a magnet for criminals and vagrants' and that Minoru Yamasaki later opined 'The low building with low density is unquestionably more satisfactory than multi-story living.' Consider whether alternative mixes of building heights or low-rise solutions would better support community safety and livability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific building features (elevators, galleries, balconies, appliances)
rubrics_metrics.description: Design features: 'skip-stop' elevators stopping only at anchor floors (1,4,7,10), large south-facing communal corridors called 'galleries', apartments without balconies, and deliberately small apartments with undersized kitchen appliances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess how these features affect everyday resident use and safety: the skip-stop elevators forced many residents to use stairs, exacerbating muggings; galleries were unpainted, dimly-lit, and became hang-outs for criminal activity; lack of balconies and small unit sizes reduced livability for larger families.

rubrics_metrics.name: Site planning and landscaping
rubrics_metrics.description: The plan called for a 'river of open space' and landscaping, but landscaping was omitted and few trees were planted; the site was bounded by decaying/abandoned nearby properties and had limited access to shopping and recreation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the surrounding urban context and on-site landscaping support the intended 'towers in the park' concept. The article notes that omission of landscaping and isolation in a 'sea of decaying and abandoned buildings' turned the surroundings into wasteland and contributed to decline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction quality and materials
rubrics_metrics.description: Overall build quality was poor: described as 'little more than steel and concrete rabbit warrens, poorly designed, badly equipped, inadequate in size, badly located, unventilated, and virtually impossible to maintain.' Ventilation was poor and maintenance problems were chronic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess material quality, ventilation, equipment, and durability. Poor construction amplified maintenance burdens and resident dissatisfaction; suppliers nevertheless marketed the project because of national exposure, masking real-quality issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Density and unit suitability
rubrics_metrics.description: Density was set at 50 units per acre (higher than downtown slums) and the complex totaled 2,870 apartments; apartments were deliberately small and few units were designed for larger families.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether density and unit mix match the demographic needs. High density coupled with small units and insufficient family-size units is flagged as a factor in poor living conditions and social stress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintenance, operations, and responsiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: The St. Louis Housing Authority had inefficient and costly maintenance; elevator breakdowns, slow response to tenant requests, and reductions in maintenance (e.g., a 10% cut) occurred. Basic services sometimes incurred extra charges to tenants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate operational capacity and maintenance funding. The article describes a feedback loop: vacancy reduced rental income, causing maintenance cuts, which further reduced desirability and increased vacancy. Timely, well-funded maintenance is presented as crucial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Financial model and funding constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: Federal cost limits and value engineering influenced design (e.g., uniform 11-floor height). The Housing Act of 1949's requirement that local housing authorities pay expenses from rental income made projects vulnerable to vacancy and fiscal problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the financing model is sustainable: Pruitt–Igoe's underfunding, rent increases (from $20 in 1952 to $58 in 1968), and charging tenants for basic services undermined affordability and maintenance. Consider impacts of federal cost constraints and local revenue dependence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy, governance, and political environment
rubrics_metrics.description: Decisions were shaped by urban renewal policy, federal agencies (Public Housing Administration, HUD), and political opposition to public housing. Segregation policies affected planning (projects were segregated until 1955). Voter opposition limited financial assistance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the political and governance context: limited political support, federal interventions, and hostile local climate are presented as key contributors to the project's inability to secure adequate funding and long-term support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Security, crime, and presence of outsiders/transients
rubrics_metrics.description: By the mid-1960s the complex was plagued by crime, particularly vandalism and juvenile delinquency; audits reported most vandalism committed by transients rather than residents; stairwells and corridors attracted muggers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess security design and management: how building form (e.g., stairwells due to skip-stop elevators, anonymous public spaces) and lack of controls invited criminal activity. Consider role of private security, its withdrawal in 1967, and the subsequent escalation in crime.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demographics and household composition
rubrics_metrics.description: High proportion of minors (a 1965 census found 69.2% of inhabitants were minors), many single-parent households (less than 30% of households with children had both parents present), large families, and high rates of out-of-wedlock births.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider demographic fit of housing design and social services: concentration of young people and single-parent families increased demand for social supports; lack thereof is implicated in juvenile delinquency and other social issues noted in the article.

rubrics_metrics.name: Community engagement and local management responses
rubrics_metrics.description: Numerous initiatives were tried (private security, rent incentives, federal grants for social programs, renovation spending), tenant organizations gained influence after a 1969 rent strike, and some apartments had residents who organized to maintain common areas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the extent and effectiveness of resident involvement and management responses: the article shows mixed results—some pockets of well-being existed where tenants organized, but many top-down interventions failed due to underfunding or scale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vacancy, occupancy, and turnover metrics
rubrics_metrics.description: Occupancy initially peaked (95% and 86%) then declined; by 1970 more than two-thirds of the complex was vacant, and at one point vacancy rates were higher than any other public housing complex in the country. Annual turnover rate was 20%.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use occupancy and turnover as leading indicators of project viability. Rising vacancy undermined revenue and triggered maintenance cutbacks, while high turnover eroded community stability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretive criteria for assessing failure (architecture vs social/political causes)
rubrics_metrics.description: The article presents competing interpretations: some critics attribute failure to architectural flaws (e.g., Charles Jencks: 'the day Modern architecture died'), while others (e.g., Katharine Bristol, Eugene Meehan) emphasize underfunding, local policy, demographic decline, and political economy as root causes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging whether a housing project 'failed' due to design, policy, or socioeconomic context, weigh architectural form against broader fiscal, managerial, and demographic factors. The page recommends avoiding monocausal explanations and considering multi-factor analyses.
